outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the only new claim bearing on the bullet is Bertalan Bodor's arXiv preprint 2507.16985 (first posted 22 July 2025, revised 13 July 2026), which proves finitely many reducts up to first-order interdefinability for every structure in one growth-rate class 𝒮; the general question stays open, no counterexample in a finite relational language has been found, and no independent engagement with the 2025 preprint was found.
problem_asks: (1) A homogeneous structure M in a finite relational language (the bullet does not say countable; the literature does). (2) M is 'finitely presented'. This phrase is not a standard term in the literature here; the nearest standard notion is 'finitely bounded' (the age of M is cut out by finitely many forbidden finite substructures, equivalently finitely many universal axioms). I record the bullet's own word and note the probable reading. (3) The question is whether M has finitely many reducts. The bullet omits 'up to first-order interdefinability', which Thomas's 1991 conjecture includes. Read literally, without that qualifier, the answer is trivially negative: (Q,<) has a reduct (Q,R_n) for each arity n, where R_n is the strict order on n-tuples, and these are infinitely many distinct structures. So the intended question is Thomas's: finitely many reducts up to first-order interdefinability. (4) The claim is universal over all such M: a counterexample is a single M in a finite relational language, finitely bounded if the bullet's word is read that way, with infinitely many reducts up to interdefinability. The Wikipedia link for 'reducts' goes to the Reduct article, which does not mention Thomas, homogeneous structures or this question.

events.what_happened: Simon Thomas, 'Reducts of the random graph', Journal of Symbolic Logic 56(1), 1991, pp. 176-181 (page numbers from the bibliography of Cameron's 2026 survey, which I opened). Classifies the first-order reducts of the random graph: five up to first-order interdefinability. Thomas conjectured that every countable homogeneous structure in a finite relational language has only finitely many reducts up to first-order interdefinability; this is the conjecture the bullet asks about. The 1991 paper itself was not opened; its statements are taken from the 2026 survey and from search-result abstracts.
events.delivers: Random graph: exactly five reducts up to first-order interdefinability, so the conjecture holds for that structure. The general conjecture is stated, not proved.
events.remains: The general conjecture for all countable homogeneous structures in a finite relational language, and every structure other than the random graph.

events.what_happened: Simon Thomas, 'Reducts of random hypergraphs', Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 80(2), 1996, pp. 165-193, DOI 10.1016/0168-0072(95)00061-5 (from a repository record and citation metadata in search results; not opened). Per the search-result abstract, it classifies the closed permutation groups between Aut(Γ_k) and Sym for the countable universal homogeneous k-hypergraph Γ_k, finds finitely many for each k, and states that each associated reduct is homogeneous in a finite relational language.
events.delivers: For each k, finitely many reducts of the random k-hypergraph up to interdefinability (counted as closed supergroups of Aut(Γ_k)). The conjecture is confirmed for these structures, which are homogeneous in finite relational languages.
events.remains: Every other homogeneous structure in a finite relational language, and the general conjecture.

events.what_happened: Markus Junker and Martin Ziegler, 'The 116 reducts of (Q,<,a)', Journal of Symbolic Logic 73(3), 2008, pp. 861-884 (citation from search results; the Freiburg preprint was listed but not opened). Per search-result summaries, it classifies the reducts of the order of the rationals with one constant a and finds 116 up to interdefinability. The date of the earlier preprint was not verified.
events.delivers: (Q,<,a), the rationals with their order and one constant, has exactly 116 reducts up to interdefinability, so the conjecture holds for that structure.
events.remains: Other expansions of (Q,<) and the general conjecture.

events.direction: Finiteness for (Q,<,a), favouring the conjecture for that structure.

events.what_happened: Péter Pál Pach, Michael Pinsker, Gabriella Pluhár, András Pongrácz and Csaba Szabó, 'Reducts of the random partial order', arXiv:1111.7109 (posted November 2011 by arXiv number; not opened), Advances in Mathematics 267 (2014) 94-120, DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2014.08.008 (citation from search results). The authors identify exactly five closed permutation groups containing the automorphism group of the random partial order, so five reducts up to first-order interdefinability; they present it as evidence for Thomas's conjecture.
events.delivers: The random partial order has exactly five reducts up to first-order interdefinability, so the conjecture holds for that structure.
events.remains: Other homogeneous structures and the general conjecture.
events.direction: Finiteness for the random partial order, favouring the conjecture for that structure.

events.what_happened: Manuel Bodirsky, Michael Pinsker and András Pongrácz, 'The 42 reducts of the random ordered graph', arXiv:1309.2165 (first posted September 2013, per search summary; not opened), Proc. London Math. Soc. 111(3) (2015), pp. 591-632, DOI 10.1112/plms/pdv037. Per the search-result abstract, the reducts of the random ordered graph (a free superposition of (Q,<) and the random graph) are classified: 42 besides the two obvious reducts (D;<,E) and (D;=), up to first-order interdefinability. The authors say the work tests Thomas's conjecture.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 Sept 2013; v2 and v3 (v3 May 2015) cited in search results; journal PLMS 2015.
events.delivers: The random ordered graph has finitely many reducts up to first-order interdefinability (42 non-trivial plus the two obvious ones), so the conjecture holds for that structure.
events.remains: Other homogeneous structures and the general conjecture.

events.what_happened: Manuel Bodirsky, Peter Jonsson and Trung Van Pham, 'The reducts of the homogeneous binary branching C-relation', arXiv:1408.2554 (posted August 2014 by arXiv number; not opened), Journal of Symbolic Logic 81(4) (2016), pp. 1255-1297, DOI 10.1017/jsl.2016.37 (citation from search results). Per the search-result abstract, the reducts of the homogeneous binary branching C-relation are finite in number up to existential interdefinability, and hence up to first-order interdefinability, which the authors say confirms Thomas's conjecture for this special case.
events.delivers: For the homogeneous binary branching C-relation (a single structure in a finite relational language), finitely many reducts up to existential, hence first-order, interdefinability.
events.remains: Other homogeneous structures and the general conjecture.

events.what_happened: Bertalan Bodor, Peter J. Cameron and Csaba Szabó, 'Infinitely many reducts of homogeneous structures', arXiv:1609.07694 (posted September 2016 by arXiv number; not opened), Algebra Universalis 79 (2018), article 43, DOI 10.1007/s00012-018-0526-8 (citation from search results). Per the search-result abstract, the countable infinite-dimensional vector space over a finite field with a constant has infinitely many first-order definable reducts, and so does the countable homogeneous Boolean algebra. Cameron's summary gives the GF(2) case, via infinite Reed-Muller-type codes.
events.delivers: Infinitely many reducts for a pointed (non-relational) vector space over a finite field and for the atomless Boolean algebra. Both signatures fall outside the finite relational hypothesis, so this shows that hypothesis is needed but does not decide the bullet's relational case.
events.remains: The bullet's case (finite relational language) is untouched by this event.
events.direction: Counterexamples to the non-relational version of Thomas's conjecture. The bullet's hypothesis is a finite relational language, so this does not contradict the bullet's statement.
events.object: Infinitely many first-order definable reducts for the countable infinite-dimensional vector space over a finite field with a distinguished constant (non-constructive in the sense that the reducts are shown to be distinct by counting; the paper's exact construction not read), and by interpretation for the countable homogeneous Boolean algebra. Cameron's summary gives the GF(2) case via infinite generalisations of binary Reed-Muller codes.

events.what_happened: Manuel Bodirsky and Bertalan Bodor, 'Structures with Small Orbit Growth', arXiv:1810.05657 (v1 12 Oct 2018; v2 25 Oct 2018; v3 17 Jan 2020), later published as 'Permutation groups with small orbit growth', Journal of Group Theory 24(4) (2021), pp. 643-709, published 20 Jan 2021 (per Dresden repository and De Gruyter listing, search results). The abstract studies the class K_exp+ of structures whose automorphism groups have at most c·n^(dn) orbits on n-tuples of pairwise distinct elements (d<1). It shows K_exp+ consists exactly of finite covers of first-order reducts of unary structures, and states: 'We also show that Thomas' conjecture holds for K_{exp+}.'
events.revisions: v1 12 Oct 2018; v2 25 Oct 2018; v3 17 Jan 2020 (current per arXiv abstract page); journal version 20 Jan 2021.
events.delivers: Every structure in K_exp+ has finitely many first-order reducts up to first-order interdefinability. Confined to the class K_exp+.
events.remains: Homogeneous structures in finite relational languages outside K_exp+, and the general conjecture.

events.direction: Finiteness for the K_exp+ class, favouring the conjecture for that class.

events.what_happened: Bertalan Bodor, 'Classification of ω-categorical monadically stable structures', arXiv:2011.08793 (single version, submitted 17 Nov 2020). Journal of Symbolic Logic 89(2) (2024), pp. 460-495, published online 19 Sept 2023 (from a search-result citation; the journal page was not opened). The abstract classifies the class M of ω-categorical monadically stable structures in terms of automorphism groups, shows every structure in M is first-order interdefinable with a finitely bounded homogeneous structure, and states: 'We also prove that every structure in M has finitely many reducts up to interdefinability, thereby confirming Thomas' conjecture for the class M.'
events.revisions: arXiv single version, 17 Nov 2020. Journal version JSL 89(2) 2024 (online Sept 2023). Not compared against the arXiv text.
events.delivers: Every structure in the class M (ω-categorical and monadically stable countable structures) has finitely many first-order reducts up to interdefinability, so the conjecture holds for M. Confined to M.
events.remains: Homogeneous structures in finite relational languages that are not in M, and the general conjecture.

events.what_happened: Manuel Bodirsky (TU Dresden), talk 'Model-theoretic challenges in Constraint Satisfaction', Freiburg logic colloquium, Tuesday 23 July 2024 (programme page opened). The abstract says the talk surveys open model-theoretic problems for homogeneous structures and their reducts that matter for CSP complexity, and names 'finite homogeneous Ramsey expansions, reconstruction of structures up to bi-interpretability from the abstract automorphism group, and Thomas's conjecture about closed supergroups' as open.
events.delivers: Nothing: a survey talk that lists Thomas's conjecture (in its closed-supergroup form) among open problems in July 2024.
events.direction: No result. Describes the conjecture as open in July 2024.

events.what_happened: Leonid Dorochko and Michał Wrona, 'Constraint Satisfaction Problems over Finitely Bounded Homogeneous Structures: a Dichotomy between FO and L-hard', arXiv:2601.22691 (v1 30 Jan 2026; v2 3 Apr 2026; v3 14 Jul 2026; abstract page opened). The abstract proves that CSPs over first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores are either first-order definable or L-hard under first-order reductions, and calls the Bodirsky-Pinsker dichotomy conjecture 'wide open'. It does not mention Thomas's conjecture. Neighbouring problem, discarded for this bullet: it is a complexity dichotomy, not a count of reducts. The full text was not read.
events.delivers: A CSP complexity dichotomy for first-order expansions of a subclass of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores. It says nothing about the number of reducts.
events.remains: Everything the bullet asks; the paper does not address it.

events.what_happened: Roman Feller and Michael Pinsker, 'Decidability of Interpretability', arXiv:2602.02302 (v1 2 Feb 2026; v2 5 Aug 2026; abstract page opened). Shows pp-bi-interpretability is decidable under mild template conditions, with background in the Bodirsky-Pinsker conjecture. The abstract does not mention Thomas's conjecture or Bodor's work. Neighbouring problem, discarded for this bullet. The full text was not read.
events.delivers: Decidability of pp-bi-interpretability for CSP templates. Not about the number of reducts.
events.remains: Everything the bullet asks; not addressed.

events.what_happened: Peter J. Cameron, 'Around homogeneity', arXiv:2602.22181 (submitted 25 Feb 2026; HTML opened), a survey dedicated to the memory of Robert Woodrow. Section 8, 'Reducts and overgroups', restates Thomas's conjecture for a homogeneous structure over a finite relational language, says 'This has been verified in a number of cases', and lists 'Question 8.1. Decide Thomas' conjecture.' In the passages read it does not mention Bodor's 2025 preprint.
events.delivers: No result. The survey restates the conjecture and lists deciding it as an open question.
events.direction: No result. Treats the general conjecture as open in February 2026.

events.what_happened: David M. Evans, 'Permutation modules for Ramsey structures', arXiv:2603.29606 (first submitted 31 Mar 2026; v2 9 Sept 2026; HTML and abstract opened). It studies permutation modules RW for automorphism groups of ω-categorical structures. In Remarks 1.3 it says that a negative answer to Question 1.2 (for finite F) 'would yield' 'a structure which is homogeneous in a finite relational language which has infinitely many first-order reducts', and that this 'would give a counterexample to a well-known conjecture of Simon Thomas [22] on reducts of finitely homogeneous structures'. Question 1.2 is left open in the paper, and its state-of-the-art reference is Yang-Bojańczyk-Klin.
events.revisions: v1 31 Mar 2026; v2 9 Sept 2026 (HTML shows v2 only).
events.delivers: No result on Thomas's conjecture. The paper identifies a conditional route by which a relational counterexample would arise, if Question 1.2 had a negative answer. It claims no such structure.
events.doubts: The counterexample remark is conditional on an open question; the paper does not claim a counterexample.
events.direction: Points to a possible relational counterexample only if a question it leaves open has a negative answer. Does not claim one.

events.what_happened: Jingjie Yang, Mikołaj Bojańczyk and Bartek Klin, 'The Finite Length Property of the Rado Graph and Friends', arXiv:2605.21681 (v1 20 May 2026; v2 9 Jul 2026; abstract page opened), accepted at LICS 2026 (DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.LICS.2026.82, per search results). The abstract proves the finite length property for (a) structures approximated by finite substructures with few orbits over fields of characteristic zero, and (b) Fraïssé limits with free amalgamation in a finite vocabulary of unary and binary relations, possibly with a generic order; the Rado graph is included. Per a search summary of the body (not verified in readable text), the paper lists 'Does every structure homogeneous over a finite relational vocabulary have the finite length property?' as open.
events.delivers: Positive finite-length results for the listed classes, including the Rado graph. Nothing about the number of reducts. It concerns the finite length question that Evans's remark would need answered negatively.
events.remains: The reducts question entirely; per the search summary, the general finite-length question for structures homogeneous over finite relational vocabularies.

events.what_happened: Bertalan Bodor, 'Structures with not too fast unlabelled growth', arXiv:2507.16985. v1 was submitted 22 July 2025 and v2 on 13 July 2026; the abstract text I opened is the current (v2) version, and the v1 abstract is the same on the claims that matter. The paper defines the class 𝒮 of countable structures whose orbit growth on n-element subsets is not faster than 2^n/p(n) for any polynomial p. It classifies 𝒮 in terms of automorphism groups, shows it has countably many structures up to bidefinability, that each is first-order interpretable in (Q,<), and that each is interdefinable with a finitely bounded homogeneous structure (and finitely homogenizable, i.e. interdefinable with a homogeneous structure in a finite relational signature). It then states: 'all structures in 𝒮 have finitely many first-order reducts up to interdefinability, thereby confirming Thomas' conjecture for the class 𝒮.' No journal reference, comment or citing paper was found.
events.revisions: v1 22 Jul 2025 19:49:17 UTC (50 KB); v2 13 Jul 2026 11:45:24 UTC (51 KB), current. The claim is the same in both abstracts as read. The v2 changes were not identified.
events.delivers: Every structure in the growth-rate class 𝒮 has finitely many first-order reducts up to interdefinability. Because each is interdefinable with a finitely bounded homogeneous structure in a finite relational signature, the claim covers the bullet's kind of object for members of 𝒮. It does not cover the general conjecture or every finitely bounded structure, since 𝒮 is defined by a growth bound and the paper does not claim it contains all such structures.
events.remains: Homogeneous structures in a finite relational language (and finitely bounded ones) with orbit growth at least 2^n/p(n) for some polynomial p, every structure outside 𝒮, and the general Thomas conjecture. Whether 'finitely presented' is meant to be wider than finitely bounded is also left open.
events.time_since_posted: about 14.5 months (v1 to 11 Oct 2026); about 3 months since v2
events.doubts: No journal listing, referee report or review was found. The paper's text was readable only up to about 100,000 of about 175,000 characters, so the classification proof and the claimed reducts count were not checked by me. The Cameron survey (Feb 2026) and the Evans paper (Mar 2026) treat the general conjecture as open, and the passages I read in each do not mention this preprint, which is a weak signal of limited uptake rather than a concern about the result. The interdefinability-to-finite-language step (finitely homogenizable) was read from the paper's Section 1.2 summary, not checked.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture (finitely many reducts up to interdefinability) for the subclass 𝒮. Favours finiteness for that subclass only. It does not settle the general question in either direction.

summary: The bullet asks whether a 'finitely presented' homogeneous structure in a finite relational language has finitely many reducts. Its literature form is Simon Thomas's 1991 conjecture, which covers every countable homogeneous structure in a finite relational language and counts reducts up to first-order interdefinability. 'Finitely presented' is not a term the literature uses here; the nearest is 'finitely bounded', and I could not establish from the bullet's source which was meant. The Wikipedia bullet has no notes and links only to the Reduct article, which does not mention Thomas. Since 26 January 2024 there is one new claim that bears on the bullet: Bodor's arXiv:2507.16985 (first posted 22 July 2025, revised 13 July 2026), which proves that every structure in one growth-rate class 𝒮 has finitely many reducts up to interdefinability, each interdefinable with a finitely bounded homogeneous structure in a finite relational signature. That is a proof for a subclass, and the paper does not claim the general conjecture. Earlier verifications, all before 2024, cover the random graph (Thomas 1991), random hypergraphs (Thomas 1996), (Q,<,a) (Junker-Ziegler 2008), the random partial order (Pach et al., arXiv 2011, Adv. Math. 2014), the random ordered graph (Bodirsky-Pinsker-Pongrácz, arXiv 2013, PLMS 2015), the binary branching C-relation (Bodirsky-Jonsson-Pham, arXiv 2014, JSL 2016), K_exp+ (Bodirsky-Bodor, arXiv 2018, J. Group Theory 2021) and the class M of ω-categorical monadically stable structures (Bodor, arXiv 2020, JSL 2024). The two counterexamples in the literature (Bodor-Cameron-Szabó 2016, Algebra Universalis 2018; the atomless Boolean algebra) use non-relational signatures and so fall outside the bullet's hypothesis. The only relational counterexample route I found is Evans's 2026 remark, which is conditional on a negative answer to an open question he leaves open. The general conjecture is still described as open in Bodirsky's July 2024 talk, Cameron's February 2026 survey (Question 8.1, 'Decide Thomas' conjecture') and Evans's March 2026 paper. I found no journal listing, review, citing paper or engagement with Bodor's 2025 preprint, and I did not read its classification proof past about 100,000 characters of roughly 175,000. Close calls: (a) Read literally, without 'up to first-order interdefinability', the question is trivially negative, because (Q,<) has a reduct (Q,R_n) for every arity n. I took the interdefinability form as intended, but the bullet's omission is a scope issue for the judging pass. (b) If 'finitely presented' means finitely bounded, the bullet covers more than 𝒮 and M, and the 2025 result covers only part of it; I could not establish whether every finitely bounded homogeneous structure in a finite relational language lies in 𝒮. (c) Expansions by constants (Junker-Ziegler, and Bodor's class 𝒮 which includes expansions of (Q,<) by finitely many constants) are counted as verified cases; a strict reading of 'finite relational language' would exclude a constant, and I did not resolve that. (d) AI: I searched explicitly for AI involvement (terms and places in the search log) and found no AI system credited with any event. The acknowledgements of Cameron (2026) and Evans (2026) credit no AI, and the readable part of Bodor (2025) has no AI statement. The pre-2024 papers were checked by abstract, metadata and search only, so their AI-free status rests on the searches and their dates. Neighbouring work recorded and set aside: Dorochko-Wrona (Jan 2026) and Feller-Pinsker (Feb 2026) concern the Bodirsky-Pinsker conjecture, and Yang-Bojańczyk-Klin (May 2026) concerns the finite-length property that Evans's remark would need. The Oberwolfach Report 58/2025 snippet describes the conjecture as a central open problem, but its PDF was not readable.
competing_reading: Read as the literature states it (every countable homogeneous structure in a finite relational language), the bullet is still open. Bodor's 2025 result and his 2020/2024 result each cover a growth-rate or stability class, so each is a partial resolution. The opposite reading: because the bullet says 'finitely presented', its class may be finitely bounded structures, and Bodor's papers show that the structures in 𝒮 and M are each interdefinable with a finitely bounded homogeneous structure in a finite relational signature. A reader could then call the bullet settled for those two classes. Neither reading makes the bullet resolved in full, but the gap between them is the scope question the judging pass has to decide.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of arXiv 2507.16985, to check the classification and the reducts count for 𝒮, the finite-relational-signature claim, and the acknowledgements. (2) A journal listing or referee history for 2507.16985, and any independent check or citation by a later paper. (3) Whether every finitely bounded homogeneous structure in a finite relational language lies in 𝒮, or whether one lies outside 𝒮 and has infinitely many reducts. (4) The exact definition of 'finitely presented' in the source the bullet was taken from, and whether the bullet's source says 'up to interdefinability'. (5) The talk content of Oberwolfach Report 58/2025 and the Thomas-related material in Bodor's JSL 2024 paper.

dead_ends: No AI-linked result on Thomas's conjecture or on reducts of homogeneous structures appeared in any search, tracker or news result. The AI-result news found concerns the Erdős unit-distance problem, Ramsey hypergraph problems and Schubert polynomials, none about reducts.
Acknowledgements of Cameron (2026) and Evans (2026) contain no AI credit (read in the HTML). The readable part of Bodor (2025) contains no AI statement, but the end of that text was not readable.

No citing paper for Bodor (2025) was found in search. Bodor, Braunfeld and Hanson (arXiv 2509.12656) was opened; its abstract mentions neither Thomas's conjecture nor reducts, and its full text was not read.
The exact-phrase search for 'not too fast unlabelled growth' returned unrelated business and medical pages.
The search for arXiv 2603.29606 by ID returned bioRxiv pages; the paper was reached by a direct fetch instead.
No Quanta Magazine article on reducts or Thomas's conjecture was found.
No Lean or Coq formalisation of reducts of homogeneous structures was found. Mathlib has basic Fraïssé theory only.
Bodirsky-Macpherson (a non-ω-categorical structure without proper reducts, answering a question of Junker-Ziegler) was seen in search. It is a different question and was not recorded as an event.
The Oberwolfach Report 58/2025 snippet describes the conjecture as a central open problem, but the PDF could not be read.
